reference.source: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle / Apley and Solomon's System of Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: A symptomatic prominence of the fifth metatarsal head on the lateral border of the forefoot, historically attributed to tailors sitting cross-legged with pressure on the outer foot
The lateral eminence causes a painful adventitial bursa, keratotic callus and skin irritation from shoe pressure, mirroring hallux valgus on the medial side

The Fallat and Coleman radiographic classification distinguishes an enlarged or laterally spurred fifth metatarsal head (type I), lateral bowing of the metatarsal shaft (type II) and a widened fourth-to-fifth intermetatarsal angle (type III, the commonest)
It frequently coexists with hallux valgus as part of a splayed forefoot, so both borders should be assessed together
Plantar or plantar-lateral keratosis suggests an associated plantarflexed or prominent fifth metatarsal head rather than a purely lateral deformity
First-line management is non-operative with wide toe-box footwear, protective padding, callus care and accommodative orthoses

When surgery is needed, the osteotomy is chosen by deformity type, ranging from lateral condylectomy for a bony spur to distal chevron or diaphyseal osteotomy to correct shaft bowing or a wide intermetatarsal angle
reference.pathophysiology: A tailor's bunion arises from a prominent lateral fifth metatarsal head, which may reflect a congenitally enlarged or laterally spurred head, congenital lateral bowing of the metatarsal shaft, or an increased fourth-to-fifth intermetatarsal angle that splays the ray outward. Chronic pressure from footwear against this prominence provokes an adventitial bursa, soft-tissue thickening and hyperkeratotic callus. Contributory biomechanical factors include a splayed forefoot with associated hallux valgus, pes planovalgus, hindfoot or forefoot varus increasing lateral loading, and ligamentous laxity. Over time the fifth toe drifts into varus while the metatarsal head deviates laterally, and abnormal plantar loading can produce an intractable plantar keratosis beneath the head.
additionalDifferentials: Hallux valgus with generalised forefoot splaying
Fifth metatarsal stress fracture or non-united avulsion at the base
Plantar or interdigital keratoma and intractable plantar keratosis
Ganglion or adventitial bursa over the metatarsophalangeal joint
Gouty tophus or inflammatory arthropathy of the fifth metatarsophalangeal joint
Soft-tissue lesion such as a lipoma or fibroma over the lateral border
additionalInvestigations: Weight-bearing dorsoplantar and oblique foot radiographs to measure the fourth-to-fifth intermetatarsal and lateral deviation angles
Assessment of the fifth metatarsal head morphology and any lateral exostosis on the oblique view
Clinical evaluation of hindfoot alignment and concurrent hallux valgus
Skin and callus mapping to localise lateral versus plantar pressure
Vascular and neurological assessment of the foot before considering surgery
Pedobarography or gait assessment where abnormal loading is suspected
redFlags: Ulceration or deep infection over the prominence, particularly in a person with diabetes or peripheral vascular disease
Sensory loss or ischaemia indicating neuropathic or vascular compromise
Rest pain, night pain or a rapidly enlarging mass suggesting a bony or soft-tissue tumour
Signs of acute inflammatory or crystal arthropathy rather than mechanical deformity
reference.prognosis: Most patients settle with footwear modification and padding, and surgical correction with an appropriately selected osteotomy gives reliable relief of the lateral prominence; recurrence and transfer plantar lesions are uncommon when the deformity type is matched to the procedure.
pitfalls: Performing an isolated condylectomy when the underlying problem is a widened intermetatarsal angle, leading to recurrence
Overlooking a coexisting plantarflexed metatarsal head and intractable plantar keratosis
Operating on a neuropathic or ischaemic foot without first assessing vascular and sensory status
Neglecting concurrent hallux valgus so the forefoot remains splayed after treatment
references: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
Apley and Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Trauma
management: First-line non-operative care with wide toe-box footwear to offload the lateral prominence
Protective padding and regular callus and skin care over the fifth metatarsal head
Accommodative orthoses to redistribute abnormal plantar and lateral loading
Simple analgesics or NSAIDs and treatment of any inflamed adventitial bursa
Surgical correction with a fifth metatarsal osteotomy selected to match the deformity type, or lateral condylectomy, when conservative measures fail
Assessment and concurrent management of coexisting hallux valgus and hindfoot malalignment
Vascular and neurological assessment of the foot before contemplating surgery
